title: Ugrasena Welcomes Krishna Back
story:
Before he left Vidarbha, Krishna told the assembled kings plainly where he was going: I shall repair to the charming city of Mathura, governed by the Bhoja king. Garuda, the son of Vinata, then asked leave of him. There is a city, the great bird said, at the base of Mount Raivata on the shore of the ocean — Kushasthali, once held by rakshasas and now abandoned, rich with flowering trees and teeming with wild creatures. Let me fly west and examine it, and see if it is worthy of your habitation. And with that he saluted Krishna and set off toward the setting sun.

Krishna, with the Yadavas, entered Mathura. The news of his imperial consecration had run ahead of him, and it had reached the old king before the man himself did. Ugrasena had heard how numberless kings had installed Krishna as emperor, how Indra had made peace with him through his envoy Chitrangada, how wealth had been apportioned so that no one who came went away empty-handed. And the king of Mathura set about preparing a welcome fit for an emperor.

He offered a great puja at the temples of the tutelary deities. He hung the gates of Vasudeva's house with flags and pennons and garlands, and decked Kamsa's old assembly hall with bright cloth. He anointed the doors of Krishna's sitting-room with sweet paste, and filled the highways with music and dancing. The whole city bloomed with flags and garlands of wild flowers and jars full of water; sandal water was sprinkled on the roads, cloth was spread on the ground, and incense of aguru burned in vessels on either side. The elderly women sang benedictions, and the young women moved through their houses in restless expectation.

Then the great conch Panchajanya sounded, and the whole of Mathura came streaming out — women, boys, elders, singers and panegyrists, and a huge army, with Balarama going before them. Ugrasena himself carried the arghya and the water for washing Krishna's feet. When the old king came within sight of Krishna, seated on a car bright with celestial jewels and shining with the wild-flower garland on his breast, he stepped down from his own white car to go the rest of the way on foot.

It does not behove me to proceed on a car after this, Ugrasena said. You go on the car.

But Krishna would not take what the old king was offering. He declined the royal arghya, and his words were gentle and final. O king of Mathura, he said, while I have installed you, declaring, Be you the lord of Mathura, it does not behove me to make it otherwise. The empire the kings had given him, the consecration the gods had performed — none of it, he meant, undid what he had already done. So get upon your white car, he told the old man, and govern the city of Mathura delightedly, with your sons and grandsons.

And to the king who had lost a son to Krishna's own hand, the conqueror spoke not of victory but of comfort. Kamsa had seized the throne and imprisoned his father; Krishna had freed Ugrasena and set him back upon it, and he would not now take the seat from him. The man who entered Mathura as an emperor left its crown exactly where he had placed it — on the head of the old king who came out on foot to meet him.
reflection: The story turns on a refusal. Krishna enters Mathura as an anointed emperor, welcomed with all the honors a king can offer — and he declines the very throne. The empire the kings and gods conferred is real, but it does not undo his earlier act: Ugrasena is lord of Mathura, and Krishna will not unmake that word. Power here is shown not by taking a crown but by refusing one he had every right to keep.
next_story_tease: But even a king of Mathura had no hall fit for the gods, and Krishna would soon ask Indra for one.
hero_scene: The elderly king Ugrasena stepping down from his white car to walk on foot toward Krishna, carrying the arghya and water for his feet, while the whole city of Mathura streams out behind him under flags and garlands.
